citation_details.author: Michael A. Jensen, Harvey Huang, Gabriela Ojeda Valencia, Bryan T. Klassen, Max van den Boom, Timothy J. Kaufmann, Gerwin Schalk, Peter Brunner, Gregory A. Worrell, Dora Hermes, Kai Joshua Miller
citation_details.abstract: Using depth electrodes in human patients, scientists at the Mayo Clinic found that the map of the body in motor cortex extends deep into the central sulcus. Unexpectedly, the nonsomatotopic ‘Rolandic motor association’ (RMA) area interrupts this organization. Cells in the precentral gyrus directly send signals to the periphery to generate movement and are principally organized as a topological map of the body. We find that movement-induced electrophysiological responses from depth electrodes extend this map three-dimensionally throughout the gyrus. Unexpectedly, this organization is interrupted by a previously undescribed motor association area in the depths of the midlateral aspect of the central sulcus. This ‘Rolandic motor association’ (RMA) area is active during movements of different body parts from both sides of the body and may be important for coordinating complex behaviors.

citation_details.author: Natalie Schaworonkow, Bradley Voytek
citation_details.abstract: In invasive electrophysiological recordings, a variety of neural oscillations can be detected across the cortex, with overlap in space and time. This overlap complicates measurement of neural oscillations using standard referencing schemes, like common average or bipolar referencing. Here, we illustrate the effects of spatial mixing on measuring neural oscillations in invasive electrophysiological recordings and demonstrate the benefits of using data-driven referencing schemes in order to improve measurement of neural oscillations. We discuss referencing as the application of a spatial filter. Spatio-spectral decomposition is used to estimate data-driven spatial filters, a computationally fast method which specifically enhances signal-to-noise ratio for oscillations in a frequency band of interest. We show that application of these data-driven spatial filters has benefits for data exploration, investigation of temporal dynamics and assessment of peak frequencies of neural oscillations.

citation_details.abstract: Intracranial brain network functional connectivity (iBNFC) quantifies the statistical dependence among neural activity of different brain regions and encodes various brain functions. RTSSC consists of multi-level intracranial iBNFC matrix reconstruction and Riemannian contrastive learning to capture iBNFC dynamic representations and reduce the dependency on labels. Our results demonstrate that RTSSC is an effective framework for modeling and decoding complex iBNFC dynamics underlying various brain functions.
